what: Enact Holdings sells private mortgage insurance. When an American buys a house with less than a twenty percent deposit, the lender usually requires insurance covering part of its loss if the borrower defaults. Enact writes that insurance and collects a monthly premium for as long as the policy stays in force.
customers: Mortgage lenders and the banks and agencies that buy the loans. The borrower pays the premium, but the lender chooses the insurer.
money: Monthly premiums on the in-force book of insured mortgages.
Returns on the investment portfolio held against future claims.
moat: Private mortgage insurance is a licensed, capital-regulated business with a handful of approved participants, and the approvals are hard to obtain. The economics are unusual and favourable: policies written years ago keep paying premiums while the house behind them has appreciated, so the risk falls every year the loan performs. Enact’s in-force book is largely made up of loans written at low rates that borrowers have no reason to refinance away.
risks: This is a credit business: its results depend on American homeowners keeping up with their mortgages, and that depends on employment.
New business volume depends on home purchases with small deposits, which have been low because mortgage rates have suppressed transactions.
House price declines would raise losses on defaults directly, because the insurance pays the gap between the loan and the sale proceeds.
Five analysts average a $47.00 target against a $44.19 price — barely 6% above, implying little expected upside.
Genworth retains a large stake, which creates an overhang and means a seller may appear at any time.
opportunities: The shares trade at about 9.2 times earnings with net income of $678.7M on a $5.9B market value, a high earnings yield.
The in-force book is unusually valuable: it was written against houses that have since appreciated, so the loan-to-value has fallen and the risk with it, while the premium keeps arriving.
High mortgage rates mean existing borrowers do not refinance, so policies persist far longer than they historically did, which extends the premium stream.
Free cash flow of $712.7M and $582.5M of cash against $752.3M of debt give a strong capital position, and the company returns capital through dividends and buybacks.
watch: The delinquency rate on the insured book. In mortgage insurance that single figure leads everything: premiums are predictable, losses are not, and delinquencies are the first visible sign of them.
view: Mortgage insurance is one of the few businesses where the passage of time makes the existing book safer rather than riskier, and that is the whole reason to look at Enact. A policy written three years ago insured a loan against a house that has since appreciated. The borrower has paid down principal. The loan-to-value that triggered the insurance requirement has fallen well below the threshold — but the premium keeps arriving every month until the policy is cancelled. The company is collecting insurance premiums on a risk that has largely gone away.

High mortgage rates have made that better rather than worse, which is counterintuitive. Borrowers sitting on loans from a cheaper era have no reason to refinance, so policies that historically cancelled after a few years are persisting far longer. Enact is earning premium on an ageing, seasoned, steadily safer book. That is a genuinely favourable position and it is not reflected in a 9.2 times earnings multiple.

The offsetting risk is the one that matters in all credit businesses: this is a bet on American homeowners continuing to pay their mortgages, which is a bet on employment. If unemployment rises materially, delinquencies follow, and mortgage insurers are geared to that in a way their steady premium income disguises. House price declines compound it, because the insurance pays the gap between the loan balance and what the house actually sells for. Both things would have to go wrong together, but they usually do.

What the low multiple also reflects is structural rather than operational: new business volume depends on first-time buyers with small deposits, and transactions have been suppressed by rates. The book is shrinking at the edges even as it seasons profitably. And Genworth’s retained stake is an overhang that could become a seller at any time. Five analysts seeing 6% upside are pricing all of that. My read is that the seasoned book is worth more than the market is paying and the new business is worth less than the bulls assume — watch the delinquency rate, monthly, and nothing else quite as closely.
bull: Rates stay high, seasoned policies persist and keep paying premiums on risk that has already fallen away, and a 9.2 times multiple on a strongly capitalised insurer re-rates.
bear: Unemployment rises, delinquencies climb on a book whose new business has already shrunk, and house price falls turn defaults into claims.
